title: Euler Tour of a Tree (Subtree Flattening)
directAnswer: An Euler tour flattens a rooted tree into an array by recording an entry time tin[node] and an exit time tout[node] during one DFS. The key property: a node's entire subtree occupies the contiguous index range [tin[node], tout[node]] in that array. That turns 'update/query a whole subtree' into 'update/query a contiguous range', so a Fenwick or segment tree over the flattened array answers subtree-sum and subtree-update in O(log n). The tour itself is O(n).

remember.pattern: DFS timestamps tin/tout so each subtree is a contiguous [tin, tout] range
rules: `tin[node]` is the node's position in the flattened array; **assign it before recursing** into children.
`tout[node]` is the **last** index belonging to node's subtree — set it after all children return.
u is an ancestor of v exactly when **tin[u] ≤ tin[v] ≤ tout[u]** — a pure range test.
Subtree of node = the contiguous slice **[tin[node], tout[node]]**, of length (tout − tin + 1) = subtree size.
Place each node's value at index `tin[node]`, then a BIT/segment tree gives subtree-sum and point/subtree updates.
whenToUse: Subtree aggregate queries or updates (sum/min/max over an entire subtree)
Ancestor / descendant tests in O(1) after an O(n) tour
Path-to-root updates combined with a difference trick on tin/tout
Reducing tree problems to array problems so 1-D structures (BIT, segment tree) apply
antiSignals: Arbitrary path (u to v) queries, not subtree → heavy-light decomposition or LCA-based splitting
The tree changes shape between queries → the tin/tout indices become stale; recompute or use a dynamic structure
Edge-based attributes rather than node-based → store edge values on the deeper endpoint, mind the off-by-one
You only need one subtree sum once → a single DFS sum is simpler than building a BIT
remember.takeaway: The Euler tour is the bridge from tree to array: one DFS assigns each subtree a contiguous index range, after which every 1-D range structure you already know (Fenwick, segment tree, prefix sums) applies to subtree queries unchanged.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can flatten a tree so subtree operations become range operations — assigning tin before recursing and tout after, and recognizing that [tin, tout] is exactly one subtree.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Setting tout before recursing (so it does not cover descendants), using a node→array map that is not contiguous, or recursing deeply enough to overflow the stack on a chain.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the contiguous-range invariant precisely, show the O(1) ancestor test, and explain how layering a Fenwick tree on the flattened array gives O(log n) subtree-sum with point updates. Mention the iterative DFS for deep trees.

problemStatement:
You are given a rooted tree with `n` nodes, each holding a value. Support:

1. ***update(node, val)*** — change the value stored at `node`.
2. ***subtreeSum(node)*** — return the sum of values over `node` and all of its descendants.

Preprocess with an Euler tour so each subtree maps to a contiguous array range, then back the array with a Fenwick tree to make both operations ***O(log n)***.
constraints: Up to 2 × 10⁵ interleaved update and subtreeSum calls
The tree is rooted and its shape is static
Sums fit in 64-bit (use long in Java)
understanding: We want subtree aggregates to be fast under updates. A subtree is awkward on a tree but trivial on an array — if only it were contiguous. The Euler tour makes it so: a single DFS that stamps an entry index when it first reaches a node and an exit index when it finishes the node's subtree lays every subtree out as one unbroken block [tin, tout]. From there, subtree operations are range operations and any 1-D range structure applies.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are queries about subtrees or arbitrary paths?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Subtrees here. The Euler tour makes a subtree contiguous. Arbitrary path queries need heavy-light decomposition or LCA splitting instead.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the tree change shape between queries?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. tin/tout indices assume a fixed shape; if edges changed we would have to recompute the tour or use a dynamic structure.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are values on nodes or edges?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Nodes here. Edge values can be pushed onto the deeper endpoint of each edge, with care about the root having no incoming edge.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How deep can the tree be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to n in a chain, so the DFS that builds the tour should be iterative (explicit stack) to avoid blowing the recursion stack at 2×10⁵.

approaches.name: Baseline — DFS the Subtree Per Query
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first: it directly answers a subtree query and exposes why repeated queries need flattening.
hints: To answer subtreeSum(node), run a DFS from node and add up every value reached — that is the subtree.
update(node, val) is a single assignment to the stored value — O(1).
But each subtree query can walk the whole tree (the root's subtree is everything) — O(n) per query, too slow for many queries.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A subtree DFS visits up to n nodes, so a query is O(n). Updates are O(1). With q queries the total is O(q·n), which is too slow when both are large.
approaches.explanation:
The direct method needs no preprocessing beyond the adjacency list.

**Update is trivial.** Storing values per node, `update(node, val)` is one write — O(1).

**Query walks the subtree.** `subtreeSum(node)` runs a DFS rooted at `node`, summing every value it reaches. Correct, because a subtree is exactly the set of nodes reachable downward from `node`.

**Why it does not scale.** A subtree can be the whole tree (querying the root), so a single query is O(n). With up to 2×10⁵ queries that is up to 4×10¹⁰ node visits.

**What flattening buys.** The subtree is reconstructed from scratch every query even though the tree shape never changes. If we instead assign each subtree a fixed contiguous range once, a query becomes a range-sum over that block — answerable in O(log n) with a Fenwick tree, and updates stay cheap.
approaches.insight: The wasted work is re-discovering the same subtree boundaries on every query. The Euler tour computes those boundaries once as [tin, tout]; everything after is a range operation on a static layout.

approaches.name: Euler Tour + Fenwick Tree (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for many subtree queries/updates. 'Flatten with tin/tout so each subtree is a range, then a BIT handles ranges.'

complexity.time: O(n) tour + O(log n) per op

hints: Run one DFS. When you first reach a node, give it tin[node] = the next free array index; when you finish its whole subtree, set tout[node] = the last index used.
Now the subtree of any node is exactly the contiguous range [tin[node], tout[node]] in the flattened array — because DFS visits a node's descendants consecutively before moving on.
Place value[node] at index tin[node]. Then subtreeSum(node) = rangeSum(tin[node], tout[node]) and update(node, v) is a point update at tin[node] — both O(log n) with a Fenwick tree.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The DFS visits each node once → O(n) to compute tin/tout and lay out the array. Each query is one range-sum (two prefix queries) and each update is one point update on the Fenwick tree → O(log n) each.
approaches.explanation:
The Euler tour rewrites the tree as an array so that the messy notion of 'subtree' becomes the clean notion of 'contiguous range'.

**Building the tour.** Run a single DFS from the root with a global counter `timer`. The instant you *enter* a node, record `tin[node] = timer` and increment `timer`; this is the node's slot in the flattened array, and we place its value there. After all of the node's children have been fully explored, record `tout[node]` as the last index that was used. Because DFS fully finishes one child's subtree before starting the next, all descendants of a node receive indices that fall between the node's own `tin` and the moment it finishes — with no outside node squeezed in.

**The contiguous-range invariant.** This is the whole point: the subtree of `node` is *exactly* the index range `[tin[node], tout[node]]`. Its length `tout[node] − tin[node] + 1` equals the subtree size. Equivalently, `u` is an ancestor of `v` iff `tin[u] ≤ tin[v] ≤ tout[u]` — an O(1) ancestor test, no walking.

**Why assign tin before recursing and tout after.** `tin` must be stamped on entry so a node sits *before* all its descendants in the array. `tout` must be stamped on exit so it captures the *last* descendant's index. Swapping the order (stamping `tout` before recursing) would make the range exclude the subtree — the classic bug.

**Layering a range structure.** With values living at `tin` positions, every subtree question is a range question:
- `subtreeSum(node) = rangeSum(tin[node], tout[node])`,
- `update(node, v)` is a point update at index `tin[node]`.

A Fenwick tree over the flattened array answers both in O(log n). A segment tree works equally well and adds range *updates* via lazy propagation (e.g. 'add x to every node in a subtree').

**Why this is the standard reduction.** Once a subtree is a contiguous range, you inherit every 1-D technique: prefix sums for static data, Fenwick/segment trees for updates, even Mo's algorithm for offline queries. The tour is the adapter that lets array tools operate on trees.
approaches.insight: The Euler tour is a coordinate change: it relabels nodes by DFS entry time so that 'descendant of u' becomes 'index in [tin[u], tout[u]]'. That single relabeling is what lets you reuse Fenwick and segment trees — structures built for arrays — on subtree problems without modification.

pitfalls: Setting tout before recursing into children — the range then excludes the subtree.
Mapping nodes to non-contiguous array slots — breaks the single-range query.
Recursive DFS on a deep chain — stack overflow; use an explicit stack.
Off-by-one between 0-based tin/tout and the 1-based Fenwick indexing.

commonMistakes: Recording tout before exploring the children, so the subtree range is incomplete.
Assuming nodes map to scattered indices instead of one contiguous block per subtree.
Using recursion on a chain-shaped tree and overflowing the stack.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: tout set too early
commonMistakesDetailed.why: tout must be the LAST index used by any descendant, so it can only be known after all children are explored. Setting it before recursing makes [tin, tout] cover just the node, dropping its subtree.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Non-contiguous node mapping
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The whole benefit is that a subtree is one contiguous range. Assigning array slots in any order other than DFS entry time scatters a subtree across the array, so a single rangeSum no longer captures it.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int slot = someHash(node);     // arbitrary positions
bitUpdate(slot, values[node]);
commonMistakesDetailed.good: bitUpdate(tin[node] + 1, values[node]);  // position = DFS entry time

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recursive DFS overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A chain of 2×10⁵ nodes recurses 2×10⁵ deep, overflowing the default stack in both Java and Python. Build the tour with an explicit stack.

patternNote: Euler tour (subtree flattening): one DFS stamps tin on entry and tout on exit so each subtree is the contiguous range [tin, tout]. This reduces subtree queries/updates and ancestor tests to array range operations, after which Fenwick or segment trees give O(log n) per operation. The standard adapter from tree problems to 1-D structures.
